vignette:
She is 61, a Latin American woman who has spent most of her adult life working behind the wheel of a city bus. She talks about driving as something she used to love for its rhythm and predictability. She knows the route by memory, knows which passengers board at the same corner every morning, knows where the road dips and where schoolchildren run too close to the curb. For years, that sense of familiarity makes her feel competent and steady. She is married, and she describes her life before the incident as busy but ordinary: early shifts, coffee in a travel mug, sore shoulders at the end of the day, dinner with her husband, television in the evening.

The event happens on a clear weekday afternoon near the end of her route. She is approaching an intersection she has crossed countless times. The light changes, traffic is moving, and she notices a young man on a bicycle trying to beat the line of cars. At the same moment, a delivery truck turns too quickly. She sees it before it happens, in that terrible stretched-out instant when she understands exactly what is about to occur and cannot do anything to stop it. She hits the brakes hard enough that passengers cry out behind her, but her bus is not the vehicle that strikes him. She watches the cyclist thrown to the pavement and dragged. She remembers the sound first-the metal, the shouting, the scream of her own brakes-more vividly even than the image. She calls dispatch and emergency services, her voice sounding strangely calm to her at the time. She is expected to stay at the scene. She sees the body lying at an angle that still returns to her unexpectedly. People gather. Someone is crying. A passenger asks her if the man is dead, and she cannot answer.

In the first days after, she tells herself she is lucky it was not her bus and that she should be able to move on. Instead, the scene begins replaying the moment she closes her eyes. She wakes in the night with her heart racing, hearing the brakes and the impact as if it is happening again outside her bedroom window. Her husband reaches for her, and she realizes she is sitting upright, already fully awake, scanning the room. She starts sleeping with the television on because silence makes the memory louder.

She returns to work quickly, partly because she needs the income and partly because staying home makes her feel weak. But driving is no longer automatic. As she approaches intersections, her hands tighten on the wheel until her knuckles ache. She slows too early, checking mirrors over and over, watching for bicycles, pedestrians, children on scooters, anything small and vulnerable near the tires of larger vehicles. If someone steps off a curb unexpectedly, a bolt of fear runs through her body so sharply that she feels nauseated. Her passengers sometimes complain that she brakes too hard now. One man mutters that she drives "like an old lady," and she feels humiliated and furious at once.

She does not like talking about what happened. At home, if her husband asks how her shift went, she says only, "Fine." She avoids the intersection where the accident happened whenever she can, even if it means taking a longer route in her own car. When road safety stories come on the news, she leaves the room. Her grandchildren want to show her videos on their phones, and if there is even a hint of traffic footage she asks them to turn it off. She used to be the one in the family who kept things moving, who organized rides, errands, birthdays. Now she startles when a car horn blares outside and snaps at people for small things, then feels ashamed.

What troubles her most is the guilt that attaches itself to details she cannot control. She replays the seconds before the collision and wonders whether she could have leaned on her horn sooner, whether stopping a little farther back might have changed something, whether she should have done more at the scene. Intellectually she knows she is not the one who hit him, but emotionally she feels implicated because she saw it, because she was there, because part of her job is to protect people on the road and she could not protect him. She says she keeps seeing his mother, though she never met her-imagining a woman waiting for a son who does not come home.

Months later, her world has become narrower. She still drives the bus, still wakes before dawn and puts on her uniform, still nods to regular passengers. From the outside she looks dependable as ever. Inside, she is braced all day. By the end of a shift, she feels as if she has been clenching every muscle in her body for hours. She is tired but dreads sleep. She tells herself to be grateful that she survived and that others have been through worse. Even so, when she nears an intersection and sees a cyclist emerge beside a truck, time slows, her chest tightens, and for a moment she is back there again, watching the moment she cannot forget.
